content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is a significant issue for women, both physically and socially. Oral treatments for HMB include antifibrinolytic drugs, which work by inhibiting enzymes in the endometrium that dissolve blood clots, thereby reducing bleeding. Historically, there has been concern that the antifibrinolytic drug tranexamic acid (TXA) might increase the risk of venous thromboembolic disease, which includes conditions such as deep vein thrombosis (blood clots in the leg veins) and pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lung vessels). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of antifibrinolytic medications in treating HMB. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases and trial registries in November 2017, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antifibrinolytics to placebo, no treatment, or other medical treatments were included. Thirteen RCTs involving 1312 participants were analyzed. The primary outcomes assessed were menstrual blood loss (MBL), improvement in HMB, and thromboembolic events. When compared to placebo or no treatment, antifibrinolytics (TXA or its prodrug Kabi) significantly reduced mean blood loss by approximately 53 mL per menstrual cycle and increased the likelihood of improvement in HMB. For example, if 11% of women improve without treatment, 43% to 63% of women taking antifibrinolytics are expected to improve. There was no clear evidence of a difference in adverse events between the groups, and only one thromboembolic event was reported across two studies. When TXA was compared to progestogens, there was no significant difference in mean blood loss, but TXA was associated with a higher likelihood of improvement in HMB. For instance, if 46% of women improve with progestogens, 61% to 83% of women are expected to improve with TXA. Adverse events were less common in the TXA group, and no thromboembolic events were reported. In comparison to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), TXA reduced mean blood loss by approximately 73 mL per cycle and increased the likelihood of improvement. If 61% of women improve with NSAIDs, 71% to 100% of women are expected to improve with TXA. Adverse events were rare, and no thromboembolic events were reported. When compared to ethamsylate, TXA reduced mean blood loss by approximately 100 mL per cycle. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of improvement or withdrawal due to adverse events. No thromboembolic events were reported. In studies comparing TXA to herbal medicines (such as Safoof Habis and Punica granatum), TXA was associated with a reduced mean PBAC (Pictorial Blood Assessment Chart) score after three months of treatment. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of improvement or adverse events. No thromboembolic events were reported. When TXA was compared to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LIUS), TXA was associated with a higher median PBAC score, indicating less effectiveness in reducing blood loss. TXA was also associated with a lower likelihood of improvement. For example, if 85% of women improve with LIUS, only 20% to 65% of women are expected to improve with TXA. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in adverse events, and no thromboembolic events were reported. In conclusion, antifibrinolytic treatment, such as TXA, appears to be effective in reducing menstrual blood loss and improving HMB when compared to placebo, NSAIDs, oral progestogens, ethamsylate, or herbal remedies. However, TXA may be less effective than LIUS. There was insufficient data to determine whether antifibrinolytics increase the risk of adverse events, including thromboembolism, as most studies did not specifically assess this outcome.
